headline: Massachusetts early voting opens Saturday ahead of Nov. 3 election
dek: Voters can cast ballots in person from Oct. 17 through Oct. 30, but locations and hours vary by city and town as nine statewide questions join the 2026 ballot.
body: Massachusetts voters can begin casting ballots in person this Saturday, Oct. 17, for the Nov. 3 state election. The early-voting period runs through Friday, Oct. 30, giving residents two weekends and nearly two weeks of weekday options before Election Day, according to the [Secretary of the Commonwealth’s official voter guide](https://www.sec.state.ma.us/divisions/elections/research-and-statistics/2026-information-for-voters/main.htm).

The election includes races for governor, the U.S. Senate and other state and district offices, as well as nine binding statewide ballot questions. The Secretary of the Commonwealth’s guide says that is the largest number of statewide questions Massachusetts voters have been asked to consider in a single election. NorthEast News has separately reported on individual questions, including proposals involving housing rules and conservation funding; voters can use the official guide to read the full text and the arguments for and against each measure.

Early voting is available without an excuse, but it is not a single statewide polling place. The [Elections Division’s instructions](https://www.sec.state.ma.us/divisions/elections/voting-information/vote-early.htm) say voters may use any early-voting location in the city or town where they are registered. That location may differ from the place assigned for Election Day, and each municipality sets its own schedule within the state’s window. The state says every city and town must offer some early-voting hours on both weekends, Oct. 17–18 and Oct. 24–25, while weekday hours may be limited or vary widely.

Local schedules are already being posted. In Revere, for example, early voting will take place at City Hall, 281 Broadway, starting Saturday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., with additional weekday and weekend sessions through Oct. 30, according to the [Revere Election Commission](https://www.revere.org/departments/election-commission). The [Revere Journal](https://reverejournal.com/2026/10/14/early-voting-in-revere-starts-on-saturday/) reported that the city’s schedule is aimed at voters preparing for the statewide races, district contests and nine ballot questions. Other cities and towns may use different buildings, hours or appointment procedures, so voters should check their local election office rather than rely on another community’s schedule.

The first deadline for people who are not registered, or who have moved, is Saturday, Oct. 24. The Secretary’s voter guide says a voter must be registered by that date to participate in the Nov. 3 election. The state directs residents to [VoteInMA.com](https://www.sec.state.ma.us/divisions/elections/research-and-statistics/2026-information-for-voters/main.htm) to register, check their information and update an address. Voters who wait until Election Day should not assume that a problem with registration or an outdated address can be fixed at the polling place without delay.

Voting by mail remains another option. The Massachusetts Attorney General’s [voter-rights guidance](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/protecting-your-right-to-vote) lists Oct. 27 as the deadline to submit a vote-by-mail application for the Nov. 3 election. The office says voters can return a ballot by mail, deliver it to their local election office or an official drop box, or bring it to an early-voting location during voting hours. The ballot must be returned under the state’s rules by Election Day, so voters who choose mail should allow time for delivery and should follow the instructions that arrive with the ballot.

On Election Day, Nov. 3, polling places will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., according to the Secretary’s guide. Election Day voters must use their assigned polling place, while early voters can use a designated location in their municipality. That distinction matters in larger communities, where a convenient early-voting site may be in a civic building or city hall rather than the school or neighborhood location used on Election Day.

For residents planning to vote this month, the practical steps are straightforward: confirm registration and address, look up the municipality’s early-voting locations and hours, and decide whether to vote in person or request a mail ballot before its deadline. The official state guide also provides the text and explanations for all nine questions. Because schedules and local instructions can change, the state and municipal election pages are the controlling sources for where and when a ballot can be cast.
